summary.text: Writing the number as \(2^k m\) with \(m\) odd, multiplicativity of the divisor sum and the perfectness identity force \(m=2^{k+1}-1\). For each \(y<n\), division \(y=am+b\) and binary expansions of \(a<2^k\) and \(b<2^{k+1}\) express \(y\) using the proper divisors \(2^i m\) and \(2^i\); the full set of proper divisors sums to \(n\), while perfectness bounds every subset sum by \(n\), so the attainable sums are exactly \(0,\ldots,n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(n)=\{d\in\mathbb N: d\mid n,\ d<n\}
\]
be the finite set of proper positive divisors of \(n\), and let
\[
S(n)=\left\{\sum_{d\in T}d:T\subseteq D(n)\right\}.
\]
Thus \(S(n)\) includes the sum of the empty subset, namely \(0\). The sequence value in the statement is
\[
a(n)=|S(n)|-1.
\]
We prove that if \(n\) is even and perfect, then in fact
\[
S(n)=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
It will then follow immediately that \(|S(n)|=n+1\) and hence \(a(n)=n\).

We first establish the arithmetic form of \(n\) that will be used in the subset-sum construction.

Write \(\sigma(r)\) for the sum of all positive divisors of a positive integer \(r\). Since \(n\) is perfect, the sum of its proper positive divisors is \(n\), and therefore
\[
\sigma(n)=2n. \tag{1}
\]
In particular, a perfect number is positive.

Because \(n\) is positive and even, we may factor out its exact power of \(2\): there are integers \(k\geq 1\) and odd \(m>0\) such that
\[
n=2^k m. \tag{2}
\]
The factors \(2^k\) and \(m\) are coprime. The divisor-sum function is multiplicative on coprime arguments, so
\[
\sigma(2^k m)=\sigma(2^k)\sigma(m).
\]
The positive divisors of \(2^k\) are \(1,2,\ldots,2^k\), and their sum is the geometric sum
\[
\sigma(2^k)=1+2+\cdots+2^k=2^{k+1}-1. \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, the geometric-sum identity follows by induction: adding \(2^{i+1}\) to \(2^{i+1}-1\) gives \(2^{i+2}-1\).

Set
\[
A=2^{k+1}-1.
\]
Combining (1), (2), and (3) gives
\[
A\sigma(m)=\sigma(2^km)=2^{k+1}m=(A+1)m=Am+m. \tag{4}
\]
Because \(m\) itself is a divisor of \(m\), we have \(\sigma(m)\geq m\). Put
\[
q=\sigma(m)-m.
\]
Equation (4) then gives
\[
Aq=m. \tag{5}
\]
Since \(k\geq1\),
\[
A=2^{k+1}-1\geq 2^2-1=3. \tag{6}
\]
As \(m>0\), equation (5) implies \(q>0\); and since \(A\geq3\), it also implies \(q<m\). Moreover, (5) says that \(q\mid m\), while by definition
\[
\sigma(m)=m+q. \tag{7}
\]
We claim that these facts force \(q=1\). Indeed, \(m\), \(q\), and \(1\) are all positive divisors of \(m\). If \(q\ne1\), then these three divisors are distinct: \(q<m\) gives \(q\ne m\), and \(m\ne1\) because \(0<q<m\). Consequently their contribution alone to \(\sigma(m)\) would be
\[
m+q+1,
\]
so \(\sigma(m)\geq m+q+1\), contradicting (7). Thus \(q=1\). Equation (5) now yields
\[
m=A=2^{k+1}-1. \tag{8}
\]
In particular, \(m\) is odd and \(m\geq3\). We have therefore obtained the needed form
\[
n=2^k m,\qquad k\geq1,\qquad m=2^{k+1}-1. \tag{9}
\]
Notice that no primality assertion about \(m\) is needed.

We next record the binary representation fact used below. For every \(r\geq0\) and every integer \(z\) with
\[
0\leq z<2^{r+1},
\]
there is a subset \(E\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,r\}\) such that
\[
z=\sum_{i\in E}2^i. \tag{10}
\]
This can be proved by induction on \(r\). For \(r=0\), the only possibilities are \(z=0\) and \(z=1\), represented respectively by the empty set and by \(\{0\}\). For the induction step, if \(z<2^{r+1}\), use the representation with exponents at most \(r\). Otherwise write
\[
z=2^{r+1}+z',\qquad 0\leq z'<2^{r+1};
\]
represent \(z'\) using exponents at most \(r\), and adjoin the exponent \(r+1\). This proves (10).

We now prove that every integer from \(0\) through \(n\) is in \(S(n)\). Let \(y\) satisfy
\[
0\leq y\leq n.
\]
There are two cases.

First suppose \(y=n\). Since \(n\) is perfect, the sum of all elements of \(D(n)\) is \(n\). Thus choosing the subset \(D(n)\) itself represents \(y=n\), so \(n\in S(n)\).

Now suppose \(y<n\). Divide \(y\) by \(m\), writing
\[
y=am+b,\qquad 0\leq b<m, \tag{11}
\]
where \(a=\lfloor y/m\rfloor\) and \(b\) is the remainder. Since \(y<n=2^km\), we have
\[
a<2^k. \tag{12}
\]
Also, by (8),
\[
b<m=2^{k+1}-1<2^{k+1}. \tag{13}
\]
Apply the binary representation fact to \(b\). There is a subset
\[
E_b\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,k\}
\]
such that
\[
b=\sum_{i\in E_b}2^i. \tag{14}
\]
Because \(k\geq1\), we may also apply the binary representation fact with largest exponent \(k-1\) to (12). Thus there is a subset
\[
E_a\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}
\]
such that
\[
a=\sum_{i\in E_a}2^i. \tag{15}
\]
Multiplying (15) by \(m\) and adding (14), we obtain
\[
y=am+b
 =\sum_{i\in E_a}2^i m+\sum_{i\in E_b}2^i. \tag{16}
\]
We must verify that the terms displayed in (16) form a subset of distinct proper divisors of \(n\).

For each \(i\leq k\), \(2^i\mid 2^km=n\). Moreover,
\[
2^i\leq2^k<2^km=n
\]
because \(m\geq3\). Hence every \(2^i\) occurring in the second sum of (16) is a proper divisor of \(n\).

For each \(i<k\), \(2^i m\mid2^km=n\), and
\[
2^im<2^km=n.
\]
Hence every \(2^im\) occurring in the first sum of (16) is also a proper divisor of \(n\).

Within either family the terms are distinct, since distinct powers of \(2\) are distinct, and multiplication by the positive number \(m\) preserves distinctness. The two families are disjoint as well. To see this, suppose that
\[
2^i=2^j m.
\]
If \(i<j\), then \(2^i<2^j\leq2^jm\), which is impossible. If \(i=j\), cancellation gives \(m=1\), contrary to \(m\geq3\). Finally, if \(i>j\), cancellation of \(2^j\) gives
\[
2^{i-j}=m.
\]
The left side is even because \(i-j>0\), whereas \(m\) is odd, again impossible. Thus there is no overlap.

Consequently, the union
\[
T_y=\{2^i:i\in E_b\}\ \cup\ \{2^im:i\in E_a\}
\]
is genuinely a subset of \(D(n)\), and by (16) its sum is \(y\). Therefore every \(y<n\) belongs to \(S(n)\). Together with the separate case \(y=n\), this proves
\[
\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\subseteq S(n). \tag{17}
\]
(The construction also covers \(y=0\): then \(a=b=0\), both binary subsets can be empty, and the resulting sum is the empty sum.)

It remains to prove the reverse inclusion. Let \(T\subseteq D(n)\). Every proper positive divisor is nonnegative, so the sum over a subset cannot exceed the sum over the whole set:
\[
\sum_{d\in T}d\leq\sum_{d\in D(n)}d.
\]
Since \(n\) is perfect, the latter sum equals \(n\). Hence every element of \(S(n)\) lies between \(0\) and \(n\), and therefore
\[
S(n)\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,n\}. \tag{18}
\]
Combining (17) and (18),
\[
S(n)=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
This set has \(n+1\) elements. The definition of \(a(n)\) removes one from this count to exclude the empty-subset sum \(0\). Thus
\[
a(n)=|S(n)|-1=(n+1)-1=n.
\]
Therefore, for every even perfect number \(n\), \(a(n)=n\), as claimed.
